lines.text: Sum of the pair, then product of the pair.
So the quadratic factor is $z^2 - 4z + 5$.

skill.title: Estimate, round and check order of magnitude

steps.title: Test each statement against a sensible height

lines.text: The shed is 8.5 m high at its highest point. A person is usually about 1.5 m to 2 m tall.
Height of Seán if the shed is 3 times as high: $8.5 \div 3 \approx 2.8$ m. This is too tall for most people.
Height of Seán if the shed is 8 times as high: $8.5 \div 8 \approx 1.06$ m. This is too short for an adult.
1.7 m is a realistic height, so tick '5 times as high as Seán'.

skill.title: Classify a function as injective, surjective, bijective

steps.title: Assume two inputs give the same output

lines.text: $f$ is injective if $f(a) = f(b)$ forces $a = b$.
Different inputs always give different outputs, so $f$ is injective.

candidates.final: f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b \text{, so } f \text{ is injective}

steps.title: (i) Follow 3 through f, then through g

lines.text: In the diagram, $f$ sends $3$ to the globe.
$g$ sends the globe to $w$.
The three elements of $B$ (plane, globe, cloud) go to three different elements of $C$: $x$, $w$ and $z$.
No element of $C$ is used more than once, so $g$ is injective.

steps.title: (ii) Show g is not surjective (not onto)

lines.text: The element $y$ in $C$ has no arrow pointing to it.
So the range $\{x, w, z\}$ is not all of $C$, and $g$ is not surjective.

skill.title: Apply Corollary 3: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle
skill.output: unknown found, justified by citing Corollary 3

steps.title: Use the angle in a semicircle

lines.text: $[AB]$ is a diameter, so the angle at $D$ on the circle is a right angle.

steps.title: (i) Explain why the angle CBD is 90 degrees

lines.text: The diagram is symmetrical about $DC$, so $[CD]$ passes through the centre of the circle and is a diameter.
$B$ is on the circle, so $\angle CBD$ is an angle at the circumference standing on the diameter $[CD]$.
The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$, so $|\angle CBD| = 90^\circ$.

steps.title: (ii) Find the first pair of equal angles

lines.text: By symmetry about $DC$, $[CD]$ is perpendicular to $[AB]$ at $E$.
So $|\angle CEB| = |\angle DEB|$ (both are $90^\circ$).

steps.title: Find the second pair of equal angles

lines.text: In triangle $BCD$, $|\angle CBD| = 90^\circ$, so $|\angle BCD|$ and $|\angle BDC|$ add to $90^\circ$.
In triangle $BED$, $|\angle DEB| = 90^\circ$, so $|\angle DBE|$ and $|\angle EDB|$ add to $90^\circ$.
So $|\angle ECB| = |\angle DBE|$.

steps.title: Find the third pair and conclude

lines.text: Angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so the remaining angles are equal: $|\angle CBE| = |\angle BDE|$.
Triangles $BCE$ and $DBE$ have all three angles equal, so they are similar.

steps.title: Find a right angle in each triangle

lines.text: $[BD] \perp [AC]$, so both triangles have a right angle at $B$.

steps.title: Use the angle in a semicircle

lines.text: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so $\angle ADC$ is $90^\circ$.

steps.title: Use the angle sum in triangle DBC

lines.text: Angles in triangle $DBC$ add to $180^\circ$ and $\angle DBC = 90^\circ$.
Both sums equal $90^\circ$ and both contain $|\angle BDC|$.
Subtract $|\angle BDC|$ from both sides.
Two angles of $ABD$ equal two angles of $DBC$ ($90^\circ$ at $B$, and $\angle ADB = \angle BCD$), so the triangles are equiangular, hence similar.
